# RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES

This chapter reviews the studies on which the research builds and identifies the gaps that it addresses. It first covers multi-task learning and negative transfer, then multi-task optimizers and their training cost, and then disaster text processing in the Philippines. It ends with a matrix that compares the key studies and a synthesis of the gaps that the research questions address.

## Multi-Task Learning and Negative Transfer

Multi-task learning trains one model on several related tasks at the same time. It is a form of inductive transfer, in which the training data of one task helps the model learn the others [@caruana1997multitask]. In natural language processing, training tasks together can help a model perform well on new data. It can also match or exceed the performance of separate single-task models while using fewer training examples [@chen2024mtlnlp].

The most widely used design is hard parameter sharing, in which all tasks share the same model parameters except the final layers that produce the output of each task [@chen2024mtlnlp]. In a language model, the shared part is an encoder, which converts each token of a text into numbers that represent its meaning in context. A task head for each task then makes the predictions for that task from these numbers [@lin2023libmtl]. Because the encoder is shared, the model reads each tweet once and uses the result for both tasks, which makes prediction faster than running two separate models [@wang2021transformer]. The encoder in this study has about 300 million parameters [@aisingapore2026sealion]. Two single-task models would therefore hold about 600 million parameters, while one multi-task model holds about 300 million plus two small task heads.

The two tasks in this study work at different levels of a tweet. Humanitarian classification works on the whole tweet and assigns it one category, such as a request for supplies or damaged infrastructure [@alam2021humaid]. Named entity recognition is a word-level task. It makes a prediction for every token and assigns an entity type to the words that name details such as places and relief goods [@ali2026humaidner]. A tweet of 30 tokens therefore receives one prediction for classification and 30 for named entity recognition. Pairing a task on the whole text with a word-level task is common in natural language processing. @weld2023survey reviewed many models that both identify the purpose of a sentence and find the details named by its words.

Training on several tasks together does not always help. A multi-task model can perform worse on a task than a model trained on that task alone, and this drop is called negative transfer [@mueller2022taskconflict; @elich2024paradigms]. Measuring it therefore requires a single-task model for each task, trained with the same encoder and setup but on one task only. @ali2026humaidner compared models on disaster tweets with two forms of the F1-score. For classification, they used macro-F1, which averages the F1-score of every category equally so that rare categories count as much as common ones. For named entity recognition, they used span-level micro-F1, which pools all entities in the test data. It counts a predicted entity as correct only when its boundaries and its type both match the label. The change on task $t$ is the score of the multi-task model minus the score of the single-task model.
$$\Delta_t = F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t} - F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}$$
A negative value of $\Delta_t$ shows negative transfer, and its size shows how much performance was lost. The average change across the two tasks is
$$\Delta_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta_1 + \Delta_2\right).$$
Studies of multi-task optimizers commonly summarize their results with a similar average change relative to single-task models [@liu2021cagrad; @navon2022bargaining; @liu2023famo]. An average, however, can hide a loss on one task behind a gain on the other. The change on each task is therefore also needed to show where negative transfer occurs.

Two causes of negative transfer are commonly described [@mueller2022taskconflict]. A gradient is the direction in which a task pushes the shared encoder to change during training. The first cause is gradient conflict, which occurs when the gradients of two tasks work against each other, so a change that helps one task harms the other [@yu2020pcgrad]. The second cause is gradient dominance, which occurs when the gradient of one task is much larger than that of the other, so the larger task controls how the model changes [@chen2018gradnorm]. The pairing of the two tasks in this study may make gradient dominance more likely. @ali2026humaidner counted up to 2,688 feedback signals per tweet for named entity recognition, from 128 token positions with 21 possible labels each, against one signal for classification.

Three disaster studies give mixed evidence on whether training on several tasks together lowers or raises performance. @ali2026humaidner trained shared encoders for both tasks on English disaster tweets, first BERT-large and then RoBERTa-large, which has 355 million parameters. With BERT-large and fixed task weights, whose values the authors did not report, classification macro-F1 peaked in the third round of training, called an epoch, and fell by 1.4 percentage points by the fifteenth. During this time, the training loss of both tasks kept falling. The authors attributed this decline to dominance by the gradients of named entity recognition, but they did not measure the gradients directly. The decline was also measured within one model over time, not against a single-task model. According to the authors, adding uncertainty weighting prevented this decline. With a schedule that later freezes the lower layers of the encoder, the best model reached 0.761 macro-F1 for classification and 0.841 span-level micro-F1 for named entity recognition. This classification score matched or exceeded the scores of 0.730 to 0.750 reported for single-task classification models, although those models were trained on the full HumAID dataset rather than on the same tweets. The study did not train a single-task model for named entity recognition, so negative transfer on that task was not measured. Its experiments also compared only fixed task weights and uncertainty weighting.

@wang2021transformer used equal weighting to train one BERT-base model to predict both the information type and the priority level of crisis tweets in the TREC Incident Streams benchmark. Compared with single-task models, the multi-task model scored lower on priority F1 (0.2544 against 0.2758) and on F1 across all information types (0.1638 against 0.1801). It scored higher on F1 for actionable information types (0.1382 against 0.1084). The authors did not report training time or memory. In this case, multi-task learning lowered the overall scores of both tasks but raised the score on the actionable information types.

Khanal and Caragea [-@khanal2021location] trained a shared BERT, ALBERT, or RoBERTa encoder for location identification, a word-level task, together with humanitarian classification and two other tasks on English crisis tweets. They used equal weighting, and each task used a different dataset rather than the same tweets. Location F1 was higher than that of the single-task model in eight of nine comparisons, with a relative gain of up to 14.76%. Only the location task was evaluated, however, so whether classification lost performance is unknown. The authors also did not report training time or memory. Across the three studies, the evidence was mixed, and each study measured only some of the tasks. None of them compared more than two multi-task optimizers, and none used Taglish. Whether any multi-task optimizer differs from equal weighting in negative transfer has therefore not been tested on Taglish tweets.

## Multi-Task Optimizers and Training Cost

Multi-task optimizers decide how the training signals of the tasks are combined into one update, which is a single change to the shared encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] divided specialized optimizers, which are all multi-task optimizers except equal weighting and tuned static weighting, into two families. Loss-based optimizers change only the weights of the task losses, so their training time stays close to that of equal weighting. Gradient-based optimizers compute the gradient of each task separately and combine the gradients into one update, which needs extra computation [@gama2026uniform]. Peitz and Hotegni [-@peitz2025multiobjective] made a similar division between methods that search for an update using the gradient of each task and methods that combine the task losses with weights.

The simplest optimizers combine the two task losses into one total loss
$$\mathcal{L} = w_1 \mathcal{L}_1 + w_2 \mathcal{L}_2,$$
where $\mathcal{L}_1$ and $\mathcal{L}_2$ are the losses of the two tasks, and $w_1$ and $w_2$ are their weights. Equal weighting gives both weights the same value [@kurin2022unitary]. Tuned static weighting also keeps the weights fixed, but it chooses their values before the final training. It tests several candidate values on validation data, which is a portion of the data kept apart for choosing settings [@xin2022mtohelp]. Random loss weighting draws new weights at random at every training step. @lin2022rlw found that it performed comparably to many specialized optimizers while running as fast as equal weighting, and they proposed it as a baseline that new optimizers should outperform.

Other loss-based optimizers adjust the weights during training. Uncertainty weighting learns a value for each task that reflects how uncertain the model is about that task, and it gives a smaller weight to the more uncertain task [@kendall2018uncertainty]. It adds only two learned values to a two-task model [@ali2026humaidner]. Gradient normalization (GradNorm) adjusts the weights so that the tasks learn at similar speeds, using the sizes of the task gradients at the last shared layer [@chen2018gradnorm]. Measuring these sizes adds some computation to each training step [@ali2026humaidner]. Fast adaptive multitask optimization (FAMO) adjusts the weights so that all task losses decrease at a balanced rate. Unlike optimizers that store the gradient of every task, it does this with memory and computation that do not grow with the number of tasks [@liu2023famo].

Gradient-based optimizers work on the task gradients directly, and some of them target gradient conflict. Projecting conflicting gradients (PCGrad) checks whether the two task gradients conflict. When they do, it removes the part of each gradient that works against the other before adding them [@yu2020pcgrad]. Gradient sign dropout (GradDrop) also targets conflict, but it works at one layer of the model. At each position in that layer, it keeps the gradients of one sign and drops those of the opposite sign. It chooses the sign at random, based on how consistent the gradients are [@chen2020graddrop].

Other gradient-based optimizers search for one update that serves all tasks. The multiple-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) finds the combination of the task gradients with the smallest size [@sener2018mgda]. To lower its cost, Sener and Koltun [-@sener2018mgda] used gradients at the output of the shared encoder instead of those of the whole encoder. This needs only a single backward pass, which is the step that computes the gradients. Conflict-averse gradient descent (CAGrad) looks for an update that improves the task that gains least, while staying close to the average of the task gradients [@liu2021cagrad]. Nash multi-task learning (Nash-MTL) treats the tasks as players that bargain over the shared update and chooses the update given by the Nash bargaining solution, a method from game theory [@navon2022bargaining]. Impartial multi-task learning (IMTL) balances both gradients and losses. It scales the task gradients so that the combined update favors neither task, and it weights the losses so that they stay at a comparable scale [@liu2021imtl].

The last optimizer in this study combines PCGrad with uncertainty weighting. Uncertainty weighting acts on the losses and may reduce gradient dominance, while PCGrad acts on the gradients and removes conflict. Because the two methods target the two causes of negative transfer described in the previous section, they may work better together than either does alone. @yu2020pcgrad used this combination on an image dataset with three tasks. @ali2026humaidner considered uncertainty weighting, PCGrad, and GradNorm, called the three methods complementary, and named a direct comparison on disaster tweets as an open direction. They chose uncertainty weighting partly because PCGrad roughly doubles memory cost, which was too high for their training setup. No earlier study reviewed here has tested this combination on text.

Earlier studies disagree on whether specialized optimizers improve on simpler methods. @xin2022mtohelp found that, on language and image tasks, specialized optimizers did not perform better than tuned static weighting. @kurin2022unitary compared equal weighting with specialized optimizers after adding common techniques that make training more stable, such as regularization. Under these conditions, equal weighting performed as well as or better than the specialized optimizers, and many remaining differences were not statistically significant. The authors argued that part of the benefit of specialized optimizers comes from a regularizing effect, which keeps the model from memorizing its training data. Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] found that in two-task problems, particularly with similar tasks, the specialized optimizers learned weights close to equal, so equal weighting approximated their behavior. Whether equal weighting matched them depended on how strongly the tasks interfered, how many tasks there were, and how much information had to be learned. They concluded that specialized optimizers remain useful for complex problems. On text, @chai2023improving found that their gradient-based optimizer, GetMTL, outperformed equal weighting, uncertainty weighting, GradNorm, and MGDA on product review and news topic classification. Their model used a small convolutional encoder rather than a transformer. Together, these studies used images, robot tasks, molecule data, machine translation, and text classification [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform; @chai2023improving]. In the text studies, all tasks were of one kind, either translation or classification of whole texts. None of the studies paired named entity recognition with classification, and none used disaster text or a code-switched language such as Taglish.

The training cost of an optimizer depends mainly on whether it computes a separate gradient for each task and for which part of the model [@lin2023libmtl; @gama2026uniform]. Most loss-based optimizers need only one backward pass, as equal weighting does. Optimizers that compute task gradients for the whole shared encoder need one backward pass per task and must store an extra copy of the gradients. Some gradient-based optimizers lower this cost by computing task gradients only at the output of the shared encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. @tbl-complexity summarizes the expected cost of the 13 optimizers based on their published descriptions. These are expected costs, not measurements.

| Optimizer | Family | Per-Task Gradients | Gradient Memory |
|:-----------------------|:-----------|:-----------------------|:-----------------|
| Equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary] | Loss | None | 1× |
| Tuned static weighting [@xin2022mtohelp] | Loss | None | 1× |
| Random loss weighting [@lin2022rlw] | Loss | None | 1× |
| Uncertainty weighting [@kendall2018uncertainty] | Loss | None | 1× |
| GradNorm [@chen2018gradnorm] | Loss | Last shared layer | Slightly over 1× |
| FAMO [@liu2023famo] | Loss | None | 1× |
| MGDA [@sener2018mgda] | Gradient | Output of the shared encoder | Slightly over 1× |
| GradDrop [@chen2020graddrop] | Gradient | One shared layer | Slightly over 1× |
| IMTL [@liu2021imtl] | Loss and gradient | Output of the shared encoder | Slightly over 1× |
| PCGrad [@yu2020pcgrad] | Gradient | Whole shared encoder | 2× |
| CAGrad [@liu2021cagrad] | Gradient | Whole shared encoder | 2× |
| Nash-MTL [@navon2022bargaining] | Gradient | Whole shared encoder | 2× |
| PCGrad with uncertainty weighting [@yu2020pcgrad; @kendall2018uncertainty] | Loss and gradient | Whole shared encoder | 2× |

: Expected training cost of the 13 multi-task optimizers for a two-task model {#tbl-complexity tbl-colwidths="[33,15,29,23]"}

Note. Per-task gradients show the part of the model for which a separate gradient is computed for each task. Gradient memory is the memory that holds the gradients of the shared encoder during training, given as a multiple of the amount used by equal weighting. A value of 2× means one extra copy of these gradients, which is about 1.2 GB for an encoder with 300 million parameters in 32-bit precision. Slightly over 1× means extra gradients for one layer or for the output of the encoder only. A few added numbers, such as learned task weights, are too small to change the value. These estimates leave out optimizer states, activations, and details of implementation. Tuned static weighting adds no memory during training, but choosing its weights requires extra training runs. The part of the model used for per-task gradients follows the published description or the common implementation in LibMTL [@lin2023libmtl].

Measured costs can be large. Across their supervised experiments, @yu2020pcgrad reported that PCGrad took up to 12 hours to finish training against 8 hours without it, and used up to 10 GB of GPU memory against 6 GB. @xin2022mtohelp observed that computing the gradient of each task lowered training speed from about 12 to about 5 steps per second. @kurin2022unitary found that equal weighting had among the lowest training times. @navon2022bargaining shortened the training time of Nash-MTL by updating its weights once every few steps, although performance sometimes dropped. The three disaster studies in the previous section reported neither training time nor memory [@ali2026humaidner; @wang2021transformer; @khanal2021location].

Training cost matters for disaster response for two reasons. First, a model trained on posts from earlier disasters often loses accuracy on a new event [@seeberger2022enhancing; @seeberger2025generalizing]. Keeping such a model useful may therefore require retraining it after new disasters, and every retraining run carries the full training cost again. Second, many groups that work in natural language processing have limited computing resources [@treviso2023efficient]. @schwartz2020green noted that the cost of computation makes deep learning research difficult for many researchers, especially those from emerging economies, and they proposed reporting computing cost alongside accuracy. Peak memory is a hard limit on such resources, because a run that needs more memory than the graphics card has stops with an error. Several optimizer studies reported training time [@yu2020pcgrad; @kurin2022unitary; @xin2022mtohelp; @navon2022bargaining; @liu2023famo], but none of those reviewed here measured both training time and peak memory for a set of optimizers on a shared language encoder.

## Disaster Text Processing in the Philippines

Crisis informatics studies how information from social media can support disaster response, and language technologies have been part of the field from its early years [@lewis2025tapping]. The main labeled datasets for the two tasks of this study are in English. HumAID contains 77,196 tweets from 19 disasters that occurred between 2016 and 2019 [@alam2021humaid]. Three crowd workers labeled each tweet with a humanitarian category, and only tweets with agreed labels were kept. CrisisBench combined eight earlier datasets into about 141,500 tweets for humanitarian classification, and its benchmark results are reported for English tweets [@alam2021crisisbench]. HUMAID-NER added entity labels to 60,000 HumAID tweets [@ali2026humaidner]. It uses 10 entity types, such as CASUALTY, REQUEST, and RESOURCE, and contains about 175,000 labeled entities. The labels follow the BIO format, which marks each token as the beginning of an entity, inside an entity, or outside any entity. With 10 entity types, this format gives the 21 possible labels per token mentioned earlier in this chapter. HumAID and HUMAID-NER contain English tweets only.

One Philippine system is designed to extract both the type of report and its details. Caoile and Aviles [-@caoile2025urdaneta] developed this system for the local government of Urdaneta City to collect comments from its official Facebook page during disasters. The system passes the comments through an extract, transform, and load pipeline to the GPT model of OpenAI. The model then detects the sentiment, emotion, intent, and urgency of each comment and extracts named entities such as places and barangay names. To avoid privacy and ethical concerns, the system was developed and tested on simulated comments. The authors reported 90.2% accuracy, with similar accuracy across Filipino, Ilocano, and Taglish inputs. Unlike the model in this study, it must send the comments to OpenAI for processing. Large language models have also improved at named entity recognition. The authors of GPT-NER reported that their approach matched fully supervised models on five standard datasets and did especially well when training data was scarce [@wang2025gptner]. They also noted that access to the model was expensive, so they reported some results on a sample of 100 test examples.

Other local government projects in the Philippines applied automated analysis to incident reports [@yaneza2025calamba; @besario2026barangay] or to transcripts of community discussions [@abisado2023legazpi] rather than to social media posts. @ramirez2026cultural analyzed Philippine social media posts by hand. They coded comments on Facebook posts about four major typhoons from 2013 to 2021 to study how cultural values shape responses to disasters, and they did not train a model. Philippine studies that trained their own models on social media posts did so for a single task. @regalado2015filiet developed FILIET, a tool for Filipino disaster tweets, and tested it on tweets from Typhoon Ruby in 2014, including code-switched ones. The tested part of the tool sorted tweets into categories such as caution and advice, casualty and damage, and donations, and a random forest reached an F-measure of 0.97 in cross-validation. A planned step that would find place names using a list of known names was not evaluated. @ermino2022urgency used 4,020 tweets about Typhoon Ulysses to train a model that classifies tweets as urgent or not urgent. The tweets were in English, Tagalog, or a mix of both, and an artificial neural network reached 99.17% accuracy on 120 validation tweets. Somido and Reyes [-@somido2023actionable] classified tweets from five Philippine disasters by whether they were informative. They noted that the slang and mixed languages in such tweets make informative ones hard to find.

Two other single-task studies dealt with news articles and with entity recognition. @regacho2023disasternews trained models to separate legitimate from fake news about Typhoon Odette (Rai) using 160 news items. @yute2021satellite collected 18,987 English and Tagalog tweets about the January 2020 eruption of Taal Volcano. They trained a named entity recognition model on 230 labeled tweets to find ashfall keywords and locations, and it reached an F-score of 0.76. None of these studies labeled the same posts for more than one task.

Code-switching is the practice of alternating between two or more languages in continuous conversation [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. Taglish, which mixes Tagalog and English, has been argued to be the everyday common language of the Philippines, and Filipino text collected from social media typically contains some code-switching [@montalan2025batayan]. Filipino, however, lacks many of the datasets, tools, and pretrained models available for English [@cruz2022tagalog], and code-switched text is itself a setting with few resources [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. Tagalog named entity recognition datasets exist, but they come from news reports, internet pages, and historical newspapers rather than from disaster posts [@miranda2023tlunifiedner; @ramos2023tfnerd; @tabuzo2026phmartiallawner]. Because the language and the available resources differ, findings from English disaster tweets may not carry over to Taglish. This applies to multi-task optimizers in particular, since Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] found that whether they help depends on the problem, such as how strongly the tasks interfere.

A model for Taglish needs an encoder pretrained on both Filipino and English. SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, developed by AI Singapore, was pretrained on 13 languages, including Filipino and English [@aisingapore2026sealion]. It follows the ModernBERT design, which was built to be fast, efficient in memory, and able to read long inputs [@warner2025modernbert]. It accepts inputs of up to about 8,000 tokens and has a vocabulary of about 262,000 entries. Filipino makes up only about 2.5% of its pretraining data, compared with about 35% for English [@aisingapore2026sealion]. The final encoder in the closest earlier study, which labeled the same tweets for both tasks, was RoBERTa-large, an English encoder with 355 million parameters [@ali2026humaidner]. Because Filipino is a small share of the pretraining data and the earlier study used a different encoder, the single-task performance of this encoder on Taglish tweets has to be measured directly.

The usefulness of a labeled dataset depends on the consistency of its labels. Inter-annotator agreement measures how often annotators who label the same items independently give the same labels. Cohen's kappa measures this agreement between two annotators on category labels and corrects for the agreement expected by chance [@cohen1960coefficient]. Landis and Koch [-@landis1977measurement] described kappa values from 0.61 to 0.80 as substantial agreement and values above 0.80 as almost perfect. Earlier disaster and Tagalog datasets reported such measures. HumAID reported agreement among its crowd workers with Fleiss' kappa and other measures [@alam2021humaid]. For Tagalog named entity recognition, @miranda2023tlunifiedner averaged over pairs of annotators and reported a Cohen's kappa of 0.81 over all tokens, 0.65 over annotated tokens only, and an F1-score of 0.91 between annotators. @tabuzo2026phmartiallawner reported a similar gap in historical Tagalog text, with a kappa of 0.86 over all tokens, 0.72 over annotated tokens, and an F1-score of 0.74 between annotators. The gap between the two kappa values in both datasets shows that the result depends on which tokens are counted. An F1-score between annotators avoids this choice by comparing whole entities. Not every dataset measured agreement, however. TF-NERD, a Tagalog dataset with 12 entity types, was labeled by one annotator, and its authors listed the lack of an agreement measure as a limitation [@ramos2023tfnerd].

No dataset found in this review labels the same Taglish posts for both humanitarian classification and named entity recognition. The Philippine datasets each carry labels for one task, and the datasets with both labels are in English. Without such a dataset, single-task and multi-task models cannot be compared on the same Taglish tweets, so negative transfer between these tasks cannot be measured.

: Algorithmic Literature Taxonomy Matrix {#tbl-matrix tbl-colwidths="[14,22,21,19,24]"}

Note. AUC is the area under the curve, a summary of classification performance. BLEU scores the quality of machine translation. BoW (bag of words) and TF-IDF (term frequency and inverse document frequency) turn text into word counts or word weights. IoU measures how much a predicted region overlaps the true region. SVM is a support vector machine. Word2vec represents each word as a list of numbers learned from text. GPU and TPU are processors used to train models. CrisisLexT26 is a set of tweets from 26 crises, and DIWATA-2 is a Philippine satellite. Mean rank is the average position of a method when all methods are ranked on each metric, and success rate is the share of robot tasks completed. $\Delta m\%$ is the average relative drop in performance compared with single-task models, where lower is better. TREC-IS is the TREC Incident Streams benchmark. XTREME is a benchmark of tasks in many languages, in which PAWS-X identifies paraphrases and POS tagging assigns the part of speech of each word. Cityscapes and NYUv2 contain street and indoor scene images, CelebA contains face images, Multi-MNIST and CIFAR-100 contain small images of digits and objects, and Office-31 and Office-Home contain object images. Amazon reviews and 20 Newsgroups contain product reviews and online discussion posts. The Waymo Open Dataset contains driving scenes, QM9 contains small molecules, and Meta-World contains robot-arm tasks.

The table shows a clear pattern. The multi-task disaster studies used English tweets. The Philippine studies used local disaster text but trained a model for one task, or sent the text to a large language model run by a private company. The optimizer studies used mostly images, robot tasks, and molecules. Their text tasks were translation, whole-text classification, or one task in several languages, and none paired a word-level task with a task on the whole text. No row combines Taglish text, both tasks, several multi-task optimizers, and measured training cost.

## Synthesis

The reviewed studies show three trends. First, the multi-task models trained for disaster tweets in the studies reviewed here used English data only [@ali2026humaidner; @wang2021transformer; @khanal2021location]. Philippine disaster studies used local text but trained models for one task [@regalado2015filiet; @ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @yute2021satellite], or sent the text to a large language model run by a private company [@caoile2025urdaneta]. Second, multi-task learning has given mixed results on disaster tasks, and each study measured only part of the effect. Under fixed task weights, classification performance fell during training when it was paired with named entity recognition [@ali2026humaidner]. Under equal weighting, a multi-task model scored lower than single-task models on both tasks overall but higher on actionable information types [@wang2021transformer]. Location identification improved when it was trained with humanitarian classification and two other tasks, but the classification side was not evaluated [@khanal2021location]. Third, many multi-task optimizers exist, but they were tested mainly on images, robot tasks, and molecules, with some work on text classification. Studies also disagree on whether they improve on simpler methods such as equal weighting [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform; @chai2023improving].

These trends leave five gaps. The four research questions address the first four in order, and the fifth is addressed by combining the answers to the third and fourth. The first gap concerns single-task scores. Because no Taglish dataset is labeled for both tasks, no single-task scores exist for both tasks on the same tweets, and negative transfer cannot be measured. The first question provides these scores. The second gap concerns the reliability of such a dataset. Earlier datasets reported the agreement of their annotators to show that their labels can be trusted [@alam2021humaid; @miranda2023tlunifiedner]. A new Taglish dataset needs the same evidence, and the second question measures it.

The remaining gaps concern the optimizers. The third gap concerns training cost. The optimizers differ in how many gradients they compute and store [@lin2023libmtl], but no study reviewed here measured both training time and peak memory for a set of optimizers on a shared language encoder. The three disaster studies reported neither [@ali2026humaidner; @wang2021transformer; @khanal2021location]. The third question measures both for all 13 optimizers. The fourth gap concerns the comparison with equal weighting. @ali2026humaidner compared only fixed task weights and uncertainty weighting on English tweets, and @wang2021transformer and Khanal and Caragea [-@khanal2021location] used equal weighting only. Whether any specialized optimizer differs from equal weighting in negative transfer has therefore not been tested on Taglish tweets. Evidence from other fields does not settle the question. @kurin2022unitary found no clear advantage for specialized optimizers, while @chai2023improving found one on text classification with a small convolutional encoder and tasks of one kind. Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] found that in two-task problems, particularly with similar tasks, specialized optimizers learned weights close to equal. They described similar tasks as having the same kind of task head, the same loss, and labels with similar distributions. The two tasks in this study differ in these respects, since one makes a prediction for each token and the other one for the whole tweet. The pairing has also shown signs of gradient dominance [@ali2026humaidner]. The fourth question identifies which optimizers, if any, differ from equal weighting under these conditions. The fifth gap concerns cost and negative transfer together. @xin2022mtohelp asked whether the extra computation of specialized optimizers could be spent more effectively, but no study reviewed here relates training cost to negative transfer for these tasks. Combining the answers to the third and fourth questions addresses this gap.

Chapter 3 describes how the study answers these questions, including how the dataset is built, how the models are trained under the same conditions, and how the results are tested for significance.
